title: 05a: Global Measures of Spatial Autocorrelation
text:
1. Getting Started
In spatial policy, one of the main development objective of the local government and planners is to ensure equal distribution of development in the province. In this case study, we are interested to examine the spatial pattern of a selected development indicator (i.e., GDP per capita) of Hunan Provice, People Republic of China, and to do the following:

To apply appropriate spatial statistical methods to discover if development are evenly distributed geographically.
If not, to find out whether there is sign of spatial clustering.
And if yes, to find out where are these clusters.

The following data sets will be used:
Hunan county boundary layer. This is a geospatial data set in ESRI shapefile format. Hunan_2012.csv: This csv file contains selected Hunan’s local development indicators in 2012.
I will now import the required packages to perform the study.

pacman::p_load(sf, spdep, tmap, tidyverse)

3. Computing Contiguity Spatial Weights
I will now use poly2nb() of spdep package to compute contiguity weight matrices for the study area. This function builds a neighbours list based on regions with contiguous boundaries. Looking at the documentation, you can pass a “queen” argument that takes TRUE or FALSE as options. If this argument is not specified, the default is set to TRUE, and will return a list of first order neighbours using the Queen criteria.

title: 04b: Spatial Weights and Applications
text:
4 Computing distance based neighbours
I will now derive distance-based weight matrices by using dnearneigh() of spdep package.
The function identifies neighbours of region points by Euclidean distance with a distance band with lower d1= and upper d2= bounds controlled by the bounds= argument. If unprojected coordinates are used, and either specified in the coordinates object x or with x as a two column matrix and longlat=TRUE, great circle distances in km will be calculated assuming the WGS84 reference ellipsoid.

4.1 Determine the cut-off distance
First, I will need to determine the upper limit for distance band:

Return a matrix with the indices of points belonging to the set of the k nearest neighbours of each other by using knearneigh() of spdep.
Convert the knn object returned by knearneigh() into a neighbours list of class nb with a list of integer vectors containing neighbour region number ids by using knn2nb().
Return the length of neighbour relationship edges by using nbdists() of spdep. The function returns in the units of the coordinates if the coordinates are projected, in km otherwise.
Remove the list structure of the returned object by using unlist().


#coords <- coordinates(hunan)
k1 <- knn2nb(knearneigh(coords))
k1dists <- unlist(nbdists(k1, coords, longlat = TRUE))
summary(k1dists)

   Min. 1st Qu.  Median    Mean 3rd Qu.    Max. 
  24.79   32.57   38.01   39.07   44.52   61.79 


The summary report shows that the largest first nearest neighbour distance is 61.79 km. Using this as the upper threshold gives certainty that all units will have at least one neighbour.


4.2 Computing fixed distance weight matrix
I will nowcompute the distance weight matrix by using dnearneigh() as shown in the code chunk below.

wm_d62 <- dnearneigh(coords, 0, 62, longlat = TRUE)
wm_d62

Percentage nonzero weights: 4.183884 
Average number of links: 3.681818

text:
6. Row-standardised Weights Matrix
Next, I will assign weights to each neighboring polygon. In our case, each neighboring polygon will be assigned equal weight using style=“W”. This is accomplished by assigning the fraction 1/(#ofneighbors) to each neighboring county then summing the weighted income values. While this is the most intuitive way to summarise the neighbors’ values, the drawback is that polygons along the edges of the study area will base their lagged values on fewer polygons thus potentially over- or under-estimating the true nature of the spatial autocorrelation in the data. For this example, we will stick with the style=“W” option for simplicity’s sake but note that other more robust options are available, notably style=“B”.

rswm_q <- nb2listw(wm_q, style="W", zero.policy = TRUE)

In this section, I will compute global spatial autocorrelation statistics and perform spatial complete randomness test for global spatial autocorrelation.

3.1 Computing Contiguity Spatial Weights
To compute global spatial autocorrelation statistics, a spatial weights matrix must first be constructed to define the spatial relationships and neighbourhood structure among the geographical units (i.e., counties) in the study area.
I will use the poly2nb() function from the spdep package to compute a contiguity-based neighbour list using shared boundary criteria. By default, the queen argument is set to TRUE, which includes all contiguous boundaries—both shared edges and single shared vertices to identify first-order spatial neighbours.

title: 04a: Network Constrained Spatial Point Patterns Analysis
text:
4. Network KDE (NKDE) Analysis
I will perform NKDE analysis by using appropriate functions provided in spNetwork package.

4.1 Preparing the lixels objects
Before computing NKDE, the SpatialLines object need to be cut into lixels with a specified minimal distance. This task can be performed using lixelize_lines() of spNetwork:

The length of a lixel, lx_length is set to 700m.
The minimum length of a lixel, mindist is set to 350m.

After cut, if the length of the final lixel is shorter than the minimum distance, it is added to the previous lixel. If NULL, then mindist = maxdist/10. Also note that the segments that are already shorter than the minimum distance are not modified.

lixels <- lixelize_lines(network, 
                         700, 
                         mindist = 375)



4.2 Generating line centre points
Next, lines_center() of spNetwork will be used to generate a SpatialPointsDataFrame (i.e. samples) with line centre points. The points are located at center of the line based on the length of the line.

samples <- lines_center(lixels) 



4.3 Performing NKDE
I will now compute the NKDE:

kernel_name argument indicates that quartic kernel is used. Possible kernel methods supported by spNetwork are triangle, gaussian, scaled gaussian, tricube, cosine ,triweight, epanechnikov and uniform.
method argument indicates that simple method is used to calculate the NKDE. Currently, spNetwork support three popular methods, they are:

method=“simple”. This first method was presented by Xie et al. (2008) and proposes an intuitive solution. The distances between events and sampling points are replaced by network distances, and the formula of the kernel is adapted to calculate the density over a linear unit instead of an areal unit.
method=“discontinuous”. The method is proposed by Okabe et al (2008), which equally “divides” the mass density of an event at intersections of lixels.
method=“continuous”. If the discontinuous method is unbiased, it leads to a discontinuous kernel function which is a bit counter-intuitive. Okabe et al (2008) proposed another version of the kernel, that divide the mass of the density at intersection but adjusts the density before the intersection to make the function continuous.



densities <- nkde(network, 
                  events = childcare,
                  w = rep(1, nrow(childcare)),
                  samples = samples,
                  kernel_name = "quartic",
                  bw = 300, 
                  div= "bw", 
                  method = "simple", 
                  digits = 1, 
                  tol = 1,
                  grid_shape = c(1,1), 
                  max_depth = 8,
                  agg = 5, 
                  sparse = TRUE,
                  verbose = FALSE)


4.3.1 Visualising NKDE
Before I can visualise the NKDE values, I will insert the computed density values (i.e. densities) into samples and lixels objects as density fields.

samples$density <- densities
lixels$density <- densities

Since svy21 projection system is in meters, the computed density values are very small i.e. 0.0000005. I will rescale the density values from number of events per meter to number of events per kilometer.

samples$density <- samples$density*1000
lixels$density <- lixels$density*1000

I will use appropriate functions of tmap package to prepare interactive and high cartographic quality map visualisation.
tmap_mode('view')
tm_shape(lixels)+
  tm_lines(col="density")+
tm_shape(childcare)+
  tm_dots()
tmap_mode('plot')
The interactive map above reveals road segments (darker colour) with relatively higher density of childcare centres than road segments with relatively lower density of childcare centres (lighter colour).

section: 5. Network Constrained G- and K-Function Analysis
text:
5. Network Constrained G- and K-Function Analysis
In this section, I will perform complete spatial randomness (CSR) test by using kfunctions() of spNetwork package. The null hypothesis is defined as:

Ho: The observed spatial point events (i.e distribution of childcare centres) are uniformly distributed over a street network in Punggol Planning Area.

The CSR test is based on the assumption of the binomial point process which implies the hypothesis that childcare centres are randomly and independently distributed over the street network.
If this hypothesis is rejected, we may infer that the distribution of childcare centres are spatially interacting and dependent on each other. As a result, they may form non-random patterns.
There are nine arguments used:

lines: A SpatialLinesDataFrame with the sampling points. The geometries must be a SpatialLinesDataFrame (may crash if some geometries are invalid).
points: A SpatialPointsDataFrame representing the points on the network. These points will be snapped on the network.
start: A double, the start value for evaluating the k and g functions.
end: A double, the last value for evaluating the k and g functions.
step: A double, the jump between two evaluations of the k and g function.
width: The width of each donut for the g-function.
nsim: An integer indicating the number of Monte Carlo simulations required. In the above example, 50 simulation was performed. Note: most of the time, more simulations are required for inference
resolution: When simulating random points on the network, selecting a resolution will reduce greatly the calculation time. When resolution is null the random points can occur everywhere on the graph. If a value is specified, the edges are split according to this value and the random points are selected vertices on the new network.
conf_int: A double indicating the width confidence interval (default = 0.05).


kfun_childcare <- kfunctions(network, 
                             childcare,
                             start = 0, 
                             end = 1000, 
                             step = 50, 
                             width = 50, 
                             nsim = 50, 
                             resolution = 50,
                             verbose = FALSE, 
                             conf_int = 0.05)

The output of kfunctions() is a list with the following values:

plotkA, a ggplot2 object representing the values of the k-function
plotgA, a ggplot2 object representing the values of the g-function
valuesA, a DataFrame with the values used to build the plots

For example, we can visualise the ggplot2 object of k-function.

kfun_childcare$plotk














NoteNote



The blue line is the empirical network K-function of the childcare centres in Punggol planning area. The gray envelop represents the results of the 50 simulations in the interval 2.5% - 97.5%. Because the blue line between the distance of 0 to 250 metres are above the gray area, we can infer that there is statistically significant spatial clustering at short distances (up to ~250 meters). There are more childcare centres located within 250 meters of one another along the network than would be expected by pure chance.

title: 01: Study on Road Accidents in Bangkok Greater Metropolitan Area
text:
Road traffic accidents are among the most persistent and spatially patterned public-safety problems facing rapidly urbanising and urbanised regions. Unlike many other point-based public-safety events, traffic accidents are constrained to occur on the road network rather than freely across the two-dimensional landscape . This structural feature of the data has direct consequences for which analytical methods are valid.
This report investigates the spatial distribution of road traffic accidents recorded in 2022 across the Bangkok Metropolitan Region (BMR), comprising Bangkok, Nonthaburi, Nakhon Pathom, Pathum Thani, Samut Prakan and Samut Sakhon. First-order and second-order spatial point pattern analysis (SPPA), with a network-constrained treatment justified by the road-bound nature of the event will be used.
Please refer to the Executive Summary for the key analysis and recommendations.

title: 01: Study on Road Accidents in Bangkok Greater Metropolitan Area
text:
2. Research Questions and Objectives
Primary research questions:

Do road traffic accidents in the BMR occur with uniform intensity across space, or are they concentrated in identifiable areas (first-order property)?
Do accidents exhibit evidence of spatial interaction, i.e., clustering, inhibition or approximate randomness, relative to an appropriate network-constrained null model (second-order property)?

Objectives:

Prepare and integrate real-world geospatial data for point-pattern analysis.
Investigate first-order properties of the traffic accident point pattern across space, using both planar (quadrat analysis) and network-constrained (Network Kernel Density Estimation) methods.
Investigate second-order properties of the accident point pattern using network-constrained methods (network K- and G-functions), reflecting the road-bound nature of the event process established in Section 1.
Critically evaluate the assumptions, methodological choices and limitations of the methods used.
Communicate findings through appropriate geovisualisation.
Translate findings into public-safety planning implications.

title: 01: Study on Road Accidents in Bangkok Greater Metropolitan Area
text:
5. First-Order Point Pattern Analysis
First-order spatial point pattern analysis for this study proceeds in two stages, reflecting the network-bound nature of road traffic accidents.
First, planar Clark-Evans test against Complete Spatial Randomness (CSR) is conducted, not as the primary evidence of clustering, but as a deliberate baseline because accidents can occur only on roads, which occupy a small fraction of the study area’s surface, a planar CSR null model is almost certain to be rejected regardless of whether genuine excess risk concentration exists. Confirming this rejection statistically therefore serves two purposes:

It establishes a quantified reference point against which the network-constrained result can later be contrasted; and
It provides direct evidence, rather than assumption, that a planar framing is inadequate for this data.

Kernel density estimation (KDE) is then applied in two forms for the same reason, i.e., a planar KDE surface is retained as an exploratory baseline, while a network-constrained KDE (NKDE) is treated as the primary first-order method, since it estimates intensity along the network itself rather than across the full 2-D plane. This avoids the systematic bias of interpreting uneven road density as uneven accident risk.

5.1 Clark-Evans Test
Method selection & justification. The Clark-Evans nearest-neighbour test is used as an initial step to check whether accidents deviate from CSR before committing to more computationally intensive methods. It compares the observed mean nearest-neighbour distance against the distance expected under a homogeneous Poisson process at the same intensity. This is appropriate as an exploratory step. As highlighted earlier, a purely planar CSR null is a naive baseline here, since accidents are structurally confined to the road network. This test is therefore used as a contrast against the network-constrained K/G-function result, not as primary evidence.
Parameters and assumptions. The Clark-Evans test measures each accident’s distance to its nearest neighbouring accident. The use of the correction = “none” argument would mean that for points near the study-area boundary, the true nearest neighbour may lie just outside the window and go undetected. Instead, the test will measure distance to a farther point that is within the boundary instead.
The alternative = “clustered” argument tests the one-sided hypothesis R < 1, which is chosen because accidents are expected to cluster around hazard-prone locations such as intersections. The test’s null model assumes a homogeneous Poisson process where every location is equally likely to have an accident. This assumption does not hold here as accidents can occur only on roads. Accident occurrence is further shaped by underlying traffic volume and population density. Both violations mean the test’s rejection of CSR should be read as evidence that a planar random-point model is the wrong lens for this data, not as direct proof of genuine excess risk concentration.
The ppp will first be re-scaled to kilometers to make the statistical output more interpretable. This is particularly relevant for accident events, as using meters may result in an output of less than one accident per meter square.

accident_ppp_km <- rescale.ppp(accident_ppp_unmarked, 1000, "km")


clarkevans.test(
  accident_ppp_km,
  correction = "none",
  clipregion = NULL,
  alternative = "clustered"
)


    Clark-Evans test
    No edge correction
    Z-test

data:  accident_ppp_km
R = 0.26385, p-value < 2.2e-16
alternative hypothesis: clustered (R < 1)


Interpretation. With an R-value of 0.26385, which is well below 1, it can be interpreted that there is strong clustering of traffic accidents. The p-value of < 0.01 indicates that the R-value is statistically significant, and thus to reject the null hypothesis of CSR. This is aligned with our expectations, since accidents are constrained to road networks.


5.2 Clark-Evans Test (Monte Carlo, 99 Simulations)
Method selection & justification. This re-runs the same test using Monte Carlo simulation, by comparing the observed R-value to the results obtained from 99 simulations of CSR conditional on the observed number of points.
Parameters and assumptions. Using nsim = 99,
sets the simulation count; the minimum achievable p-value at this setting is 1/(99+1) = 0.01, which is exactly what was obtained — meaning the observed pattern was more extreme than every single simulated CSR realisation. The same CSR/independence assumptions as the analytic test apply to each simulated realisation.

clarkevans.test(
  accident_ppp_km,
  correction = "none",
  clipregion = NULL,
  alternative = "clustered",
  method = "MonteCarlo",
  nsim = 99
)


    Clark-Evans test
    No edge correction
    Monte Carlo test based on 99 simulations of CSR with fixed n

data:  accident_ppp_km
R = 0.26385, p-value = 0.01
alternative hypothesis: clustered (R < 1)


Interpretation. With the same R-value of 0.26385 and p-value of 0.01 (smallest value achieveable by nsim = 99), the same interpretation can be made. As the conclusion is made using a simulation-based method, the findings is made more robust.


5.3 Bandwidth Selection for Kernel Density Estimation (KDE)
Bandwidth the most consequential parameter in KDE. Too small and the surface just reproduces individual points (noise, not pattern), while too large and it smooths away real local hotspots into one vague blob. Since density() requires an indicated bandwidth, a check will be done on four different functions for computing bandwidth.
The bandwidth will be calculated using the four methods and plotted for visual inspection.

bw.diggle(accident_ppp_km)

0.02307687 

bw.CvL(accident_ppp_km)

7.06346 

bw.scott(accident_ppp_km)

5.200235 4.063834 

bw.ppl(accident_ppp_km)

0.7507077 



kde_diggle <- density(accident_ppp_km, sigma = bw.diggle, edge = TRUE)
kde_cvl    <- density(accident_ppp_km, sigma = bw.CvL, edge = TRUE)
kde_scott    <- density(accident_ppp_km, sigma = bw.scott, edge = TRUE)
kde_ppl    <- density(accident_ppp_km, sigma = bw.ppl, edge = TRUE)

par(mfrow = c(2, 2))
plot(kde_diggle, main = "bw.diggle")
plot(kde_cvl, main = "bw.CvL")
plot(kde_scott, main = "bw.scott")
plot(kde_ppl, main = "bw.ppl")








Interpretation. Comparing the four bandwidth selectors visually rather than by their sigma values alone reveals a clearer picture. bw.diggle and bw.ppl (0.023 km and 0.75 km respectively) both produce maps that trace the underlying road network, with narrow bright lines following street shapes rather than distinct hotspot regions. This indicates under-smoothing, where the estimate at each location is driven by only the handful of nearest accident points. bw.CvL and bw.scott (7.06 km and ~4-5 km) instead collapse the pattern into a single broad, diffuse blob covering a large area. This indicates over-smoothing.
None of the bandwidth selector produces a map suited to identifying discrete, actionable hotspots. This demonstrates that a purely planar kernel density approach struggles to find a bandwidth that meaningfully separates “accident risk” from “road network shape” in data that is inherently constrained to the road network.
bw.ppl is selected as the working bandwidth for the exploratory planar KDE baseline as it is the least extreme under-smoother and the closest to providing some accident point details. The output is treated as a baseline for comparison rather than the primary first-order evidence. This finding directly reinforces the report’s methodological decision to rely on Network KDE (NKDE) as the primary first-order method, since NKDE smooths intensity along the network itself and is therefore not subject to the same trade-off between tracing the road pattern and diffusing it into a blob.

6. Spatial Correlogram
Spatial correlograms are great to examine patterns of spatial autocorrelation in data or model residuals. They show how correlated are pairs of spatial observations when you increase the distance (lag) between them, by plotting some index of autocorrelation (Moran’s I or Geary’s c) against distance. Although correlograms are not as fundamental as variograms (a keystone concept of geostatistics), they are very useful as an exploratory and descriptive tool. For this purpose they actually provide richer information than variograms.

title: 05b Local Measures of Spatial Autocorrelation
text: Local Measures of Spatial Autocorrelation (LMSA) examine the relationships between individual spatial units and their immediate surroundings. Instead of relying on a single summary statistic across an entire geographic region, local measures provide specific scores to uncover underlying spatial structures. Key examples include Local Indicators of Spatial Association (LISA), which mathematically decompose global spatial autocorrelation into local components—and Getis-Ord’s Gi-statistics, both of which provide valuable insights for detecting local spatial clustering in spatial data.

3. Local Indicators of Spatial Association(LISA)
LISA are local spatial statistics used to evaluate the presence of spatial clusters and outliers in geographically referenced data. When examining spatial attributes such as GDP per capita across Hunan province, local spatial clustering indicates that specific counties exhibit values significantly higher or lower than would be expected under spatial randomness. This section demonstrates how to calculate and interpret LISA statistics, specifically Local Moran’s I to identify spatial clusters and outliers using GDPPC data from Hunan Province.

3.1 Computing Contiguity Spatial Weights
Before we can compute the local spatial autocorrelation statistics, we need to construct a spatial weights of the study area. The spatial weights is used to define the neighbourhood relationships between the geographical units (i.e., county) in the study area.

wm_q <- hunan %>%
  mutate(nb = st_contiguity(geometry),
         wt = st_weights(
           nb, style = "W"),
         .before = 1)

3.3.1 Mapping local Moran’s I values
Using choropleth mapping functions of tmap package, I can plot the local Moran’s I values.

3.3.2 Mapping local Moran’s I p-values
The choropleth shows there is evidence for both positive and negative I values. However, it is useful to consider the p-values for each of these values.
I will produce a choropleth map of Moran’s I p-values by using functions of tmap package.

              fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(

tmap_arrange(ii.map, p_ii.map, asp=1, ncol=2)










3.3.4 Preparing and Visualising LISA Map
Visualising LISA involves generating spatial representations that highlight statistically significant spatial patterns, including spatial clusters (high-high or low-low values) and localised spatial outliers (high-low or low-high values). Standard approaches include choropleth maps displaying local statistics, Moran scatterplots to depict spatial autocorrelation at individual locations, and hot spot analysis maps.A LISA Cluster Map classifies statistically significant locations according to their specific spatial autocorrelation type. Prior to generating this cluster map, a Moran scatterplot is constructed to examine spatial relationships. By plotting a standardized spatial variable on the x-axis against its spatial lag on the y-axis, the scatterplot’s regression slope corresponds to the global Moran’s I. The four resulting quadrants delineate high-high and low-low spatial clusters, as well as high-low and low-high spatial outliers. The spatial lag, which represents the weighted average attribute value of neighboring locations, can be computed using the st_lag() function from the sfdep R package.

lisa <- lisa %>%
  mutate(lag_GDPPC = st_lag(
    GDPPC, nb, wt),
    .before = 1) %>%
  unnest(lag_GDPPC)

I will now plot the Moran Scatterplot of GDPPC against its spatial lag version

ggplot(data = lisa, 
       aes(x = GDPPC, 
           y = lag_GDPPC)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", 
              se = FALSE, 
              color = "red") +
  labs(x = "GDPPC",
       y = "Spatial Lag of GDPPC",
       title = "Moran Scatterplot") +
  theme_minimal()








The Moran Scatterplot above is not very intuitive and visualisation is required for communication of analysis.

ggplot(data = lisa, 
       aes(x = GDPPC, 
           y = lag_GDPPC, 
           color = mean)) +
  geom_point(size = 2) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", 
              se = FALSE, 
              color = "black") +
  geom_hline(yintercept=mean(lisa$lag_GDPPC), lty=2) + 
    geom_vline(xintercept=mean(lisa$GDPPC), lty=2) +
  scale_color_manual(
    values = c("High-High" = "red", 
               "Low-Low" = "blue",
               "Low-High" = "lightblue", 
               "High-Low" = "pink")) +
  labs(x = "GDPPC",
       y = "Spatial Lag of GDPPC",
       title = "Moran Scatterplot with LISA Quadrants") +
  theme_minimal()










3.3.5 Plotting Moran scatterplot with standardised variable
I will use scale() to center and scale the variable. Centering is done by subtracting the mean (omitting NAs) in the corresponding columns, and scaling is done by dividing the (centered) variable by their standard deviations.

lisa <- lisa %>%
  mutate(z_GDPPC = scale(GDPPC),
         z_lag_GDPPC = scale(lag_GDPPC),
         .before = 1)

The as.vector() added to the end is to make sure that the data type we get is a vector, that maps neatly into out dataframe.
I am now ready to plot the Moran scatterplot again.

ggplot(data = lisa, 
       aes(x = z_GDPPC, 
           y = z_lag_GDPPC, 
           color = mean)) +
  geom_point(size = 2) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", 
              se = FALSE, 
              color = "black") +
  geom_hline(yintercept=mean(lisa$z_lag_GDPPC), lty=2) + 
    geom_vline(xintercept=mean(lisa$z_GDPPC), lty=2) +
  scale_color_manual(
    values = c("High-High" = "red", 
               "Low-Low" = "blue",
               "Low-High" = "lightblue", 
               "High-Low" = "pink")) +
  labs(x = "Standardised GDPPC",
       y = "Standardised Spatial Lag of GDPPC",
       title = "Standardised Moran Scatterplot with LISA Quadrants") +
  theme_minimal()










3.3.6 Preparing LISA map classes
I will derive the spatially lagged variable of interest (i.e. GDPPC) and center the spatially lagged variable around its mean. This is follow by centering the local Moran’s around the mean.
Thereafter, I will set a statistical significance level for the local Moran.

signif <- 0.05       



3.3.7 Plotting and visualising LISA map
By default, the LISA classes are stored in mean, median and pysal fields of lisa sf data frame. To prepare the LISA map, I will derive a new field called LISA-cluster from either one of these three field and plot the LISA map.

lisa <- lisa %>%
  mutate(
    LISA_cluster = ifelse(
      p_ii < 0.05,
      as.character(mean), 
      "Insignificant"),
    LISA_cluster = factor(
      LISA_cluster,
      levels = c("Insignificant", "Low-Low", "Low-High", "High-Low", "High-High")

      position = tm_pos_in("left", "bottom"))
  ) +
  tm_borders() +
  tm_title("Local Moran's I Clusters (p < 0.05)")
lisa_map

title: 05b Local Measures of Spatial Autocorrelation
section: 4. Hot Spots and Cold Spots Analysis (HCSA)
text:
4. Hot Spots and Cold Spots Analysis (HCSA)
Hot Spot and Cold Spot Analysis (HCSA) is a spatial statistical technique used to detect statistically significant spatial clusters of high values (hot spots) and low values (cold spots) for a geographically referenced attribute, such as GDPPC. By identifying areas where values are concentrated far more densely than expected under spatial randomness, HCSA provides critical insights into spatial structure. Specifically, a hot spot represents a region where high attribute values are spatially aggregated and surrounded by neighboring locations that also exhibit high values. Conversely, a cold spot denotes an area where low values are clustered among equally low neighboring values. To evaluate whether observed spatial patterns are statistically significant or merely random variations, HCSA utilises local spatial statistics, primarily Getis-Ord’s Gi* statistic. The complete analytical workflow consists of four core steps:

Deriving a spatial weight matrix.
Computing Gi* statistics.
Mapping Gi* statistics.
Communicating the analysis results.


4.1 Deriving distance weight matrix
While spatial autocorrelation considered units that shared borders, Getis-Ord Gi* statistics uses neighbours defined based on distance.
There are two types of distance-based proximity matrix:

fixed distance weight matrix,
adaptive distance weight matrix, and
inverse distance weights.


4.1.1 Computing fixed distance weights
In this section, I will compute fixed distance weight matrix by using st_dist_band() and st_weights() of sfdep package.
First, we need to determine the upper limit for distance band by using the steps below:

ct <- critical_threshold(st_geometry(hunan))
ct

[1] 60799.91


The summary report shows that the largest first nearest neighbour distance is 60.80 km. Using this as the upper threshold gives certainty that all units will have at least one neighbour.
Using the critical threshold value computed above, I will compute the fixed distance weight.

hunan_fdw <- hunan %>% 
  mutate(nb = include_self(
    st_dist_band(
      st_geometry(geometry), 
                 upper = ct)),
    wt = st_weights(nb, 
                      style = "W"),
    .before = 1) 



4.1.2 Computing adaptive distance weights
One of the characteristics of fixed distance weight matrix is that more densely settled areas (usually the urban areas) tend to have more neighbours and the less densely settled areas (usually the rural counties) tend to have lesser neighbours. Having many neighbours smooth the neighbour relationship across more neighbours.
It is possible to control the numbers of neighbours directly using k-nearest neighbours, either accepting asymmetric neighbours or imposing symmetry.
In this section, I will compute fixed distance weight matrix by using st_dist_band() and st_weights() of sfdep package.

hunan_adw <- hunan %>%
  mutate(nb = include_self(
    st_knn(
      st_geometry(geometry),
      k = 6)),
    wt = st_weights(
      nb, style = "W"),
    .before = 1)




4.2 Computing local Gi*
Local Gi* is a Getis-Ord statistic used in spatial analysis to identify statistically significant hot spots and cold spots of high or low attribute values within a dataset. It measures the spatial clustering of values by comparing the total value within a specified neighborhood to the global total, producing a Z-score and p-value for each location to determine the likelihood that the observed pattern is not due to random chance.
In this sub-section, I will be performing Gi* analysis by using local_gstar_perm() of sfdep package.

HCSA_fdw <- hunan_fdw %>%
  mutate(
    gistar = local_gstar_perm(
      GDPPC, nb, wt, nsim = 99),
    .before = 1) %>%
  unnest(gistar)



4.3 Preparing and Visualising HCSA Map

4.3.1 Mapping Gi* with fix distance weights
I will be using thematic mapping functions of tmaps to prepare a choropleth map showing the distribution of Gi* values.

tm_shape(HCSA_fdw) +
  tm_polygons(fill = "gi_star",
              fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(
                style = "pretty",
                n = 6,
                values = "brewer.rd_bu"),
              fill.legend = tm_legend(
                title = "Gi*",
                position = tm_pos_out())) + 
  tm_borders(fill_alpha = 0.5) +
  tm_title("Gi* of GDPPC (Fixed Bandwidth d = 60799.91m)")










4.3.2 Mapping local Gi* p-values
The choropleth shows there is evidence for both positive and negative I values. However, it is useful to consider the p-values for each of these values.
I will plot a choropleth map of p-values of Gi* by using functions of tmap package.

tm_shape(HCSA_fdw) +
  tm_polygons(fill = "p_sim", 
              fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(
                breaks = c(-Inf, 0.001, 0.01, 0.05, 0.1, Inf),
                values = "-brewer.Reds"),
              fill.legend = tm_legend(
                title = "simulated p-value",
      position = tm_pos_out())) + 
  tm_borders(fill_alpha = 0.5) +
  tm_title("p-values of local Gi* of GDPPC (Fixed distance)")










4.3.3 Mapping both Gi* values and p-values
For effective interpretation, it is better to plot both the Gi* values map and its corresponding p-values map next to each other.

Gi_star_map <- tm_shape(HCSA_fdw) +
  tm_polygons(fill = "gi_star",
              fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(
                style = "pretty",
                n = 5,
                values = "-brewer.rd_bu"),
              fill.legend = tm_legend(
                title = "local Gi*",
                position = tm_pos_in(
                  "left", "bottom"))) + 
  tm_borders(fill_alpha = 0.5) +
  tm_title("Local Gi* of GDPPC")

p_values_map <- tm_shape(HCSA_fdw) +
  tm_polygons(fill = "p_sim", 
              fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(
                breaks = c(0, 0.001, 0.01, 0.05, 0.1, 1),
                values = "-brewer.reds"),
              fill.legend = tm_legend(
                title = "p-value",
      position = tm_pos_in("left", "bottom")
    )) + 
  tm_borders(fill_alpha = 0.5) +
  tm_title("p-values of local Gi* of GDPPC (fixed distance)")

tmap_arrange(Gi_star_map, p_values_map, asp=1, ncol=2)











4.3.4 Plotting and visualising HCSA Map
By default, the HCSA classes are stored in cluster field of HCSA_fdw sf data frame. To prepare the HSCA map, I will derive a new field called HCSA_cluster from cluster field and plot the HCSA map.

HCSA_fdw <- HCSA_fdw %>%
  mutate(HCSA_cluster = case_when(
    p_sim > 0.05 ~ "Insignificant",
    p_sim <= 0.05 & cluster == "High" ~ "Hot spot",
    p_sim <= 0.05 & cluster == "Low"  ~ "Cold spot",
    TRUE ~ "Other"),
    HCSA_cluster = factor(
      HCSA_cluster,
      levels = c("Insignificant", "Hot spot", "Cold spot")
    ),
    .before = 1
  )


HCSA_map <- tm_shape(HCSA_fdw) + 
  tm_polygons(
    fill = "HCSA_cluster",
    fill.scale = tm_scale_categorical(
      values = c(
        "grey80",      # Insignificant
        "red",        # Low-Low
        "blue"          # High-High
      )
    ),
    fill.legend = tm_legend(
      title = "HSCA Cluster",
      position = tm_pos_in("left", "bottom"))
  ) +
  tm_borders() +
  tm_title("HCSA Clusters (p < 0.05)")
HCSA_map








For effective interpretation, it is better to plot both the local Gi* values map and its corresponding HCSA map next to each other.

tmap_arrange(Gi_star_map, HCSA_map, asp=1, ncol=2)

3.3 Data-Quality Handling Applied to Point Events:
To prepare the data sets for analysis, the following data-quality handling was applied for the traffic accident point event data set thai_road_accident_2019_2022.csv:

Filtering out point events within boundary and temporal points in 2022: (see section 4.3.2) Based on the province names under province_en and incident_datetime, observations outside the study area and temporal period are filtered out.
Missing values: (see section 4.3.4) There are 189 records that are missing latitude and longitude data in the data set, which were filtered out.
Erroneous values: (see section 4.3.4) Under the field number_of_vehicles_involved, there were five records indicating zero vehicles were involved in the traffic accident. The details were explored and these appeared to be data entry errors as the accident descriptions mentioned collisions. These five records were treated as data entry errors but retained, considering there woould not be any analysis involving number of vehicles.
Duplicate observations: (see section 4.3.4) Using the values in acc_code which provided a unique ID for each traffic accident, the distinct() function was used to check and remove any duplicate event point. There was no duplicate event point identified.
Invalid coordinates or geometries: (see section 4.4) Four event points that were misaligned or located outside the study area were dropped by subsetting the ppp point object against the owin object.
Overlapping observations: (see section 4.4) Even after removing duplicate observations, there might be point events of different traffic accidents that overlap. Using rjitter(), any identified overlapping point events would be moved by one meter.

title: 01: Study on Road Accidents in Bangkok Greater Metropolitan Area
text:
5. First-Order SPPA
To examine the first-order spatial distribution of road traffic accidents in BMR, a planar Quadrat Analysis is conducted as a primary exploratory step. A network-based quadrat method segments the road network in order to aggregate point events along it (Shiode, 2008). However, it appears to be appropriate only for a smaller geometry boundary. Using the quadratcount() from spadstat.linnet package on the BMR road network resulted in about 250,000 line segments, which was computationally challenging to run as no output was produced even after more than 10 minutes (Baddeley et al., n.d.). Instead, a planar quadrat analysis was conducted to evaluate spatial variation and test for Complete Spatial Randomness (CSR) using a Chi-square goodness-of-fit test.
Complementing this, Network Kernel Density Estimation (NKDE) is applied. Traffic accidents are constrained to linear transport infrastructure rather than freely distributed across 2D space. NKDE adapts conventional density estimation by calculating accident intensity along network segments using shortest-path network distances rather than Euclidean distances (Okabe et al., 2009). Combining network-adjusted quadrat partitioning with NKDE prevents false density artifacts in planar spaces, offering a realistic representation of traffic accident risk along BMR’s road networks.

5.1 Quadrat Analysis
Method Selection: Quadrat analysis was selected as an initial exploratory step because it provides two things the later methods do not, i.e., a significance test (Chi-square goodness-of-fit) that directly quantifies deviation from CSR with a p-value, and an explainable intensity surface that can be cross-checked against road length per cell to distinguish areas of accident concentration from areas that simply have more road exposure.
To detect non-random accident clustering across a road network, quadrat analysis divides the study area into a grid and compares observed cell counts against a Poisson distribution CSR using Chi-square.
Parameter and Assumption: An 8×8 grid was used, balancing the ability to detect localised variation against the Chi-square test’s requirement that expected cell counts not be too small. As the BMR boundary is irregular, st_intersection() clipping means edge quadrats are genuinely smaller than interior ones. intensity() accounted for this using each quadrat’s actual clipped area. The test’s null hypothesis assumed a homogeneous Poisson process, where accidents occur independently and with equal probability anywhere in the study area.

5.1.1 Chi-square quadrat test
The quadratcount() from spadstat package was used to divid the study area into an 8 x 8 grid and count the number of accident point events in each cell.

qcount <- quadratcount(accident_ppp_km, nx = 8, ny = 8)

qcount_intensity <- intensity(qcount)

quadrat.test(accident_ppp_km, nx = 8, ny = 8)


    Chi-squared test of CSR using quadrat counts

data:  accident_ppp_km
X2 = 6223.5, df = 58, p-value < 2.2e-16
alternative hypothesis: two.sided

Quadrats: 59 tiles (irregular windows)


With a p-value of < 0.05 from the chi-square quadrat test, the null hypothesis of CSR is rejected. This indicates that traffic accidents are not uniformly distributed across the BMR under a planar model, which is expected given that accidents are confined to a road network.


5.1.2 Plotting Accident Intensity
An 8×8 rectangular grid was generated over the BMR boundary and clipped to its irregular extent using st_intersection(), so quadrats along the study area’s edge reflect their true partial area. Accident counts per quadrat were obtained using st_intersects(), and intensity was calculated as accident count divided by each quadrat’s clipped area in km².






NoteAI Use Disclosure



AI tools were used to draft the R code for constructing the 8 × 8 quadrat grid over the BMR boundary and calculating accident intensity (accidents per km²) per quadrat. The output was reviewed and run by the author to verify correctness against the study data.

  st_filter(bmr, .predicate = st_within)

grid_bmr <- st_make_grid(bmr, n = c(8, 8)) %>%
  st_sf(quadrat_id = seq_along(.), geometry = .) %>%
  st_intersection(bmr)

grid_bmr <- grid_bmr %>%
  mutate(
    accident_count = lengths(st_intersects(., accident_bmr)),
    area_km2 = as.numeric(st_area(.)) / 1e6,
    intensity = accident_count / area_km2

To verify the visual observation, road segments were clipped to each quadrat using st_intersection() and their lengths measured using st_length(). group_by() and summarise(sum()) were then used to compute total road length per cell. Dividing accident count by road length would show how many accidents occur per kilometre of road, so cells with elevated risk could be told apart from cells that simply have a denser road network.

Interpretation: Together, these results provide consistent evidence against a planar CSR model. The Chi-square quadrat test rejects CSR (p < 0.05), and the 8×8 intensity map identifies a specific area of concentration at the bottom right of BMR, i.e., quadrat 23, coinciding with Suvarnabhumi Airport. This concentration was not due to denser road networks. Quadrat 23 recorded the highest accident rate per kilometre of road (1.24) despite having a smaller road network than several neighbouring cells, indicating genuine excess risk rather than proportional exposure. As anticipated, however, planar quadrat analysis treated the entire study area as available space, which is not the case for a network-bound process. This limitation motivates the network-constrained NKDE analysis that follows, which estimates intensity only along the network itself.



5.2 Network Kernel Density Estimate (NKDE)
Method Selection: NKDE was selected as it estimates density using shortest-path distances along the network rather than Euclidean distances across the 2D plane, directly addressing the network-bound nature of traffic accidents. Unlike planar KDE, it cannot mistake road network density for accident risk, since intensity is calculated only at locations where accidents can actually occur.
Parameter and Assumption: A lixel length of 200m and minimum distance of 50m, following the standard example provided in the spNetwork package documentation (Gelb, 2025), were initially considered. However, given the substantially larger scale of the BMR network compared to the single-city network used in that reference example, a coarser lixel length of 400m and minimum distance of 200m was adopted instead as a practical trade-off between spatial resolution and tractability.
NKDE assumes the road network accurately represents where accidents can occur, and that bandwidth was appropriately sized to reveal genuine structure rather than noise or an over-smoothed trend. As roads outside the main-road classes were excluded from the network, accidents on minor roads were snapped to the nearest main-road segment during network construction, introducing some positional error at that scale.

5.2.1 Preparing lixel objects
Before NKDE could be computed, the road network was split into short, roughly equal-length segments called lixels. This provided a consistent spatial unit along the network at which density could be sampled. method = “discontinuous” was used, which corrects the bias present in the “simple” method, where an event’s mass is multiplied rather than divided at intersections (Sugihara et al., 2010). This produces an unbiased but discontinuous surface, adopted here over the smoother “continuous” method as a more computationally optimised choice.
As the BMR network is substantially larger than the package’s reference example (Gelb, 2025), spNetwork’s built-in strategies for large data sets were used.

grid_shape, which partitions the study area into a grid (with a buffer to avoid edge effects at cell boundaries) so computation proceeds cell-by-cell rather than across the whole network at once.
agg = 5, which aggregates events within a 5m radius before computing density, reducing the effective number of distinct points without materially affecting results at this resolution.
multisession() from the future package was used to further optimise computation across available cores.


lixels_bmr <- lixelize_lines(roads_bmr, 400, mindist = 200)
samples_bmr <- lines_center(lixels_bmr)

future::plan(future::multisession(workers = 10))  

nkde_bmr <- nkde.mc(
  lines = roads_bmr,
  events = accident_bmr,
  w = rep(1, nrow(accident_bmr)),
  samples = samples_bmr,
  kernel_name = "quartic",
  bw = 500,
  method = "discontinuous",
  div = "bw",
  digits = 1,
  tol = 1,
  grid_shape = c(10, 10),
  max_depth = 8,
  agg = 5,
  sparse = TRUE,
  verbose = FALSE
)

future::plan(future::sequential) 

samples_bmr$density <- nkde_bmr

samples_bmr_sf <- st_as_sf(samples_bmr) %>%
  mutate(density_scaled = density * 1000) %>%
  arrange(density_scaled)



5.2.2 Plotting NKDE
A fixed bandwidth of 500m was used, chosen because full data-driven bandwidth selection was too slow to run at BMR’s scale. Instead, 500m was obtained from the spNetwork package’s own bike-accident example (Gelb, 2025), where cross-validation found an optimal bandwidth of around 550 to 600m, and an adaptive-bandwidth approach found around 450 to 500m using the same discontinuous method used here. As this is a similar urban road-accident dataset, 500m offers a reasonable, evidence-informed estimate.

tm_shape(bmr) + tm_polygons(col = "grey95") +
  tm_shape(roads_bmr) + tm_lines(col = "grey70", lwd = 0.2) +
  tm_shape(samples_bmr_sf) +
  tm_dots(
    fill = "density_scaled",
    fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(style = "kmeans", n = 7, values = rev(RColorBrewer::brewer.pal(7, "Spectral"))),
    fill.legend = tm_legend(title = "NKDE Density (×1000)"),
    size = 0.2
  ) +
  tm_layout(
    main.title = "Network KDE of Accidents",
    main.title.size = 1,
  )








Interpretation: The NKDE plot shows density concentrating heavily along a small number of specific roads, with the brightest red segments appearing along the same area surfaced in the quadrat analysis finding in Section 5.1.2. This road-based detail is a pattern the quadrat method could only capture at the resolution of an 8×8 grid, while NKDE was able to surface individual road segments, showing that risk is not spread across the general area but tied to specific stretches of road. The majority of the network remains at very low density (blue), including most of the western BMR, again consistent with the quadrat findings.

title: 01: Study on Road Accidents in Bangkok Greater Metropolitan Area
text:
6. Second-Order SPPA
While the first-order SPPA evaluated large-scale variations in event intensity across the study area, the second-order analysis examined small-scale spatial interactions and distance dependencies between the accident events themselves. This was to determine whether road traffic accidents in the BMR exhibited significant spatial clustering, spatial dispersion or CSR across varying distance scales. This tests whether the occurrence of an accident at a specific location influences the probability of other accidents occurring nearby. Given the road-bound nature of accidents, the network-constrained K-function and its nearest-neighbour counterpart, the G-function, are used, evaluating the observed pattern against a null model of complete spatial randomness on the network itself, rather than across the unconstrained 2D plane.

6.1 Network K-Function Analysis
Method Selection: Network K-function analysis was selected because the standard planar K-function’s assumption of an infinitely continuous 2D space, with distances measured as straight-line Euclidean distance, does not hold for traffic accidents, which are geocoded to and constrained by the road network. Under this constraint, the relevant question is not whether accidents deviate from randomness across the full plane, but whether they deviate from randomness within the network itself, with distances measured as shortest-path network distance rather than Euclidean distance (Yamada & Thill, 2004). This directly extends the network-constrained reasoning already established for NKDE in Section 5.2, from a density surface to a formal test of spatial interaction between events.
Parameter and Assumption: Monte Carlo simulation was used to empirically estimate the sampling distribution, comparing the observed K-function against 20 random realisations of points placed uniformly along the network rather than against an analytically derived benchmark. The test’s null hypothesis assumes CSR on the network, i.e. that accidents are equally likely to occur at any location along the road network and occur independently of one another. This differs from the planar CSR assumption used in Section 5.1, which treats the entire study area as available space; the network-constrained null model instead only requires deviation to be assessed relative to where accidents can actually occur.
Ho: The observed spatial point events (i.e., traffic accidents) are uniformly distributed over a street network in BMR.
A simulation count of nsim = 19 was used for computational optimisation given the network’s size. This gives a minimum achievable p-value of 1/(nsim+1) = 0.05, enough to detect a clear rejection of network CSR, consistent with the strong clustering already found in Section 5.1. The trade-off is a coarser confidence envelope, estimated from only 19 simulated curves rather than a larger number, which limits precise interpretation if results fall close to the envelope boundary rather than clearly outside it.

6.1.1 Computing the Network K-Function
start = 0 and end = 2000 were selected to test clustering at scales from the immediate network vicinity up to roughly four times the NKDE bandwidth (500m; Section 5.2.2), allowing comparison of whether clustering persists beyond the scale already revealed by density estimation, while remaining within a distance range still meaningful for targeted public-safety intervention. step and width were both set to 200m, giving 10 evenly-spaced distance bands across this range, a resolution fine enough to locate the approximate distance at which clustering becomes non-significant, without excessive computation time at metro scale.

set.seed(267)

kfun_bmr <- kfunctions(roads_bmr,
                        accident_bmr,
                        start = 0,
                        end = 2000,
                        step = 200,
                        width = 200,
                        nsim = 19,
                        resolution = 200,
                        verbose = FALSE)


kfun_bmr$plotk








Interpretation: The observed blue line sits definitively above the simulation envelope across the entire 0 to 2000m range tested. The null hypothesis is thus rejected. The blue line also steadily increases with distance, indicating that clustering compounds uniformly. This means accidents are far more clustered together than a network-random pattern would produce, and this holds at every distance scale.



6.2 Network G-Function
Method Selection: While the K-function is cumulative, summing all event pairs within a given distance, the G-function instead uses nearest-neighbour distances, making it sensitive to local clustering e.g., accidents occurring very close to one another, such as at a single junction. Running both K- and G-functions provides a check on each other. If the G-function shows strong short-range clustering while the K-function’s signal is concentrated at similarly small distances, this corroborates a genuinely local hotspot effect rather than a broader network-level pattern that only appears clustered when aggregated cumulatively.
Parameter and Assumption: As the K- and G-functions are computed together in a single kfunctions() call, the same parameters and assumptions described in Section 6.1 apply here.

kfun_bmr$plotg








Interpretation: The observed blue line sits definitively above the simulated envelope, across the entire 0 to 2000m range tested. The null hypothesis is thus rejected. The gap between the line and envelope is slightly higher below 500m distance, with a sharp spike slightly below 250m. This indicates that accidents happen below 500m of another accident far more often, particularly at about 250m.
Both K- and G-functions corroborates, and substantially strengthens, the first-order findings from quadrat analysis and NKDE. Accidents in the BMR are not merely following where roads are, or even where roads are especially dense, but are genuinely clustering at every scale examined, particularly at distances below 500m, particularly at about 250m.

title: 01: Study on Road Accidents in Bangkok Greater Metropolitan Area
text:
7. Value-Added Analysis
The first- and second-order analysis established that accidents in the BMR cluster significantly beyond what network geometry alone would predict, with the strongest signal concentrated in quadrat 23, where Suvarnabhumi Airport is located. This section extends these findings using two methods to addresss two questions the first- and second-order analyses could not answer on their own:

Is quadrat 23’s extreme accident rate a statistically significant spatial outlier relative to its immediate surroundings, or does it simply reflect the same local variation expected by chance.
Do the most severe accidents cluster in the same locations as accidents overall, or do they exhibit a distinct spatial pattern.

Both questions carry direct implications for how the public-safety planning recommendations in Section 8 should be scoped and targeted.

7.1 Local Moran’s I
Method Selection: Local Indicators of Spatial Association (LISA) through Local Moran’s I was used to classify each spatial unit relative to its neighbours. High-High and Low-Low indicate a genuine cluster, while High-Low and Low-High indicate a spatial outlier. This method was selected because it directly tests whether quadrat 23’s elevated accident rate reflects a broader area cluster, consistent with the network-wide clustering in Section 6, or a localised outlier. This is a distinction Sections 5 and 6 could not resolve, since they either treat the network as one continuous space (K/G-functions) or measure exposure without reference to neighbouring areas (Section 5.1.2). The classification is examined through the standardised Moran scatterplot, alongside the underlying ii statistic and its significance.
Parameter and Assumption: Queen contiguity is used to define neighbours using st_contiguity(), with row-standardised weights style = “W”. A simulation count of nsim = 999 is used. The method assumes the spatial weights matrix appropriately represents meaningful spatial relationships between quadrats, where edge quadrats with fewer neighbours, as noted in Section 5.1, may yield less stable local estimates than interior quadrats.

pacman::p_load(sfdep)


wm_q <- grid_bmr %>%
  mutate(nb = st_contiguity(geometry),
         wt = st_weights(
          nb, style = "W"),
         .before = 1)

summary(wm_q$nb)

    intensity, nb, wt, nsim = 999),
    .before = 1) %>%

lisa %>%

  tm_polygons(fill = "ii",
              fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(
                style = "pretty",
                n = 5,
                values = "brewer.RdBu"),
              fill.legend = tm_legend(
                title = "Local Moran's I",
                position = tm_pos_out())) +
  tm_borders(fill_alpha = 0.5) +

p_ii.map <- tm_shape(lisa) +

tmap_arrange(ii.map, p_ii.map, asp = 1, ncol = 2)








Interpretation: Local Moran’s I identifies a large, statistically significant High-High cluster spanning 9 contiguous quadrats across the central to southern-eastern BMR, including quadrat 23 (ii = 5.00, p < 0.05).

lisa <- lisa %>%
  mutate(
    z_intensity = scale(intensity) %>% as.vector(),
    z_lag_intensity = st_lag(z_intensity, nb, wt)
  )

ggplot(data = lisa,
       aes(x = z_intensity,
           y = z_lag_intensity,
           color = mean)) +
  geom_point(size = 2) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm",
              se = FALSE,
              color = "black") +
  geom_hline(yintercept = mean(lisa$z_lag_intensity), lty = 2) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = mean(lisa$z_intensity), lty = 2) +
  scale_color_manual(
    values = c("High-High" = "red",
               "Low-Low" = "blue",
               "Low-High" = "lightblue",
               "High-Low" = "pink")) +
  labs(x = "Standardised Accident Intensity",
       y = "Standardised Spatial Lag of Accident Intensity",
       title = "Standardised Moran Scatterplot of Accident Intensity",
       color = "LISA Quadrant") +
  theme_minimal()









lisa %>%
  st_drop_geometry() %>%
  filter(quadrat_id == 23) %>%
  select(quadrat_id, z_intensity, z_lag_intensity, mean)

# A tibble: 1 × 4
  quadrat_id z_intensity z_lag_intensity mean     
       <int>       <dbl>           <dbl> <fct>    
1         23        4.68            1.05 High-High


Interpretation: The scatterplot shows clear separation into groups rather than a uniform scatter: Low-Low quadrats cluster tightly in the lower-left, while High-High quadrats separate distinctly in the upper-right, visually confirming the significant clustering found above. Quadrat 23 has by far the highest standardised intensity (z = 4.68), but a lower lag intensity compared to its neighbours (z = 1.05). This reinforces the cluster finding that quadrat 23 is the most severe point within a cluster, rather than an isolated spike inflating an otherwise average neighbourhood.
This corroborates the network K/G-function findings in Section 6, that clustering is not confined to a single point but extends across a wider area, consistent with the K-function’s distance-independent result. It also adds a distinction the earlier road-length comparison in Section 5.1.2 could not make on its own. Rather than being a High-Low outlier standing apart from its surroundings, quadrat 23 sits within a broader region of similarly elevated risk. Its disproportionate accident rate relative to road length remains real, but occurs within, not despite, this wider cluster.
Together, the three analyses point to the same conclusion at increasing spatial resolution. Accidents concentrate in a specific area (Section 5.1), cluster with one another at every distance tested (Section 6), and form a genuine multi-quadrat cluster rather than an isolated anomaly (Section 7.1). This supports an area-wide intervention across the identified cluster, rather than one scoped to quadrat 23 alone.


7.2 Network Cross-K/G Function: Fatal vs Non-Fatal Accidents
Method Selection: The network K/G-function analysis in Section 6 treated all accidents as a single, undifferentiated point pattern. This section extends that analysis using spNetwork’s bivariate cross-K/G function, which tests whether two distinct point types, i.e., fatal and non-fatal accidents, are spatially associated with one another along the network, beyond what their individual frequencies alone would predict. This was not covered in the core exercise and directly extends the network-constrained second-order framework already established in Section 6. This addresses a materially different and more policy-relevant question on whether the most severe accidents cluster in the same locations.
Parameter and Assumption: Accidents are split into two groups using number_of_fatalities > 0, using a binary treatment, since fatalities are a rare and heavily zero-inflated outcome. The same network roads_bmr, distance range (start = 0, end = 2000), and resolution settings used in Section 6.1 are retained for direct comparability between the univariate and bivariate results. Given the substantially smaller number of fatal accidents relative to non-fatal accidents, nsim = 19 is used for the same computational reasons as Section 6.1. The null hypothesis assumes that, given the fixed locations of non-fatal accidents on the network, fatal accidents are randomly and independently distributed.






NoteAI Use Disclosure



AI tools were used to draft the R code for classifying accidents into fatal and non-fatal groups (based on number_of_fatalities). The output was reviewed and run by the author to verify correctness against the study data.



accident_bmr <- accident_bmr %>%
  mutate(fatal = if_else(number_of_fatalities > 0, "Fatal", "Non-fatal"))

accident_fatal <- accident_bmr %>% filter(fatal == "Fatal")
accident_nonfatal <- accident_bmr %>% filter(fatal == "Non-fatal")

nrow(accident_fatal)

[1] 158

nrow(accident_nonfatal)

[1] 3431



set.seed(267)

cross_kfun <- cross_kfunctions(roads_bmr,
                                accident_fatal,
                                accident_nonfatal,
                                start = 0,
                                end = 2000,
                                step = 200,
                                width = 200,
                                nsim = 19,
                                resolution = 200,
                                verbose = FALSE)


cross_kfun$plotk









cross_kfun$plotg








Interpretation: Both the cross-K and cross-G functions reject spatial independence between fatal and non-fatal accidents, with observed values remaining above the simulation envelope across the entire 0 to 2,000m range. Fatal accidents consistently occur closer to non-fatal accidents than random co-location would predict, most strongly at short range, as observed in the cross-G function’s early peak at about 250m, which shows fatal accidents frequently have a non-fatal accident as an immediate nearest neighbour.
This means the hotspot area is not just where accidents are frequent, but where severe and less-severe accidents occur alongside each other.

8. Public-Safety Planning and Management Implications

8.1 Summary of Analysis
The analyses in Sections 5 to 7 converge on a consistent finding. Road traffic accidents in the BMR are not randomly distributed, nor do they simply follow road network density. Quadrat analysis (Section 5.1) identified a specific area of concentration, i.e., quadrat 23 where Suvarnabhumi Airport, with an accident rate per kilometre of road roughly 2.6 times higher than the next-highest quadrat. This indicated a disproportion road exposure alone cannot explain. NKDE (Section 5.2) resolved this concentration to specific networks rather than the whole area. Network K/G-functions (Section 6) confirmed accidents cluster with one another at every distance tested up to 2km, and Local Moran’s I (Section 7.1) confirmed this is a genuine multi-quadrat cluster, not an isolated anomaly. The cross-K/G analysis (Section 7.2) further showed fatal accidents are not spatially separate from this pattern, as they occur consistently near non-fatal accidents, most strongly at short range.
A specific corridor spanning several contiguous quadrats around quadrat, plausibly associated with Suvarnabhumi Airport access infrastructure, is a genuine statistical concentration of both accident frequency and severity, not an artefact of road density or chance.


8.2 Recommendations
Emergency response and resource allocation: Given the confirmed cluster’s spatial extent (Section 7.1) rather than a single point, pre-positioning ambulance or traffic-police resources across the identified network is directly supported by the evidence. The fatal/non-fatal co-clustering finding (Section 7.2) further supports treating this network as a priority for reducing response time specifically, since severe outcomes are concentrated exactly where accident volume is highest. However, selecting the specific road segments or stations for resource pre-positioning would require additional information not present in this dataset, such as real-time traffic congestion patterns, peak-hour travel times and existing response-unit coverage.
Road-safety and infrastructure planning: Quadrant 23’s disproportionate accident rate relative to its road length (Section 5.1.2), smaller network, higher rate, suggests engineering review, i.e., signage, speed enforcement, intersection design, is warranted there specifically, ahead of areas with more road-km but proportionally fewer accidents. This is a reasonable planning priority, but not evidence that any specific design flaw causes the pattern, which would require site-level engineering assessment beyond this data set.
Resource allocation across the BMR. The cold spot in the north-western BMR indicates comparatively lower accident-related demand there. This can inform relative prioritisation of accident-focused resources, though it should not be read as evidence of lower risk per unit of exposure, e.g., per vehicle-km, which this analysis does not measure.
Required additional information: the specific causal mechanism behind the corridor’s excess risk, e.g., airport-related traffic conflict, road geometry and driver behaviour, is not identified by this analysis and would require site-level investigation. Land-use and long-term infrastructure planning decisions would need traffic volume and exposure data this study does not include. This study also does not claim that the identified provinces or roads are inherently more dangerous per unit of traffic, only that raw and network-adjusted accident concentration is elevated there in 2022.

9. Methodological Limitations
Analytic & Data Constraints

Road Network Simplification: Restricted to main road classes (motorway, trunk, primary, secondary, tertiary), excluding minor/service roads.
Coordinate Data Quality: 189 records with missing coordinates were dropped, and 4 points fell outside the study boundary despite being labelled within it — some residual geo-referencing imprecision may remain.
No Exposure Normalisation: Accident counts are not adjusted for traffic volume or vehicle-km; elevated intensity may partly reflect exposure rather than per-unit risk.
Temporal Aggregation: 2022 accidents were analysed as a single static pattern; seasonal and day-of-week patterns were not explored.
Attribute Depth: Analysis focuses on location and network topology; available attributes such as weather and road description were not incorporated spatially.

9. Public-Safety Implications & Recommendations

Public-Safety ImplicationsRecommendations


Targeted Enforcement: Deploy automated speed cameras and traffic enforcement along identified high-density NKDE arterial corridors rather than uniform district distribution.
Optimized EMS Placement: Position Emergency Medical Services (EMS) response units near critical inter-provincial highway interchanges to cut emergency response times.
Engineering Audits: High-density accident corridors highlight structural road engineering flaws (e.g., risky lane merges, poor lighting, or missing pedestrian crossings).


Prioritise Infrastructure Audits: Focus road safety investments and structural redesign on top-quantile NKDE risk corridors.
Dynamic Spatiotemporal Models: Expand SPPA modeling to include temporal slicing (rush-hour vs. overnight and rainy season).

text:
7. Key Spatial Findings
Spatial Distribution & Intensity

Non-Random Network Clustering: Accidents are strongly concentrated in the central to south-eastern BMR road networks.
Co-Location of Severity: Cross-K/G analysis shows fatal accidents consistently cluster near non-fatal crashes at short range.
Network vs. Spatial Resolution: Network KDE successfully refined broad area concentrations (from Quadrat analysis) down to specific high-risk road segments.

Network Constraints & Clustering

Statistically Significant Clustering: Network K-function simulations confirm significant spatial aggregation across multiple network distance bands (p < 0.05).
Local Spatial Autocorrelation: Local Moran’s I confirms these high-intensity segments represent quadrat clusters rather than isolated outliers.

7. Spatially Constrained Clustering: SKATER approach
I will be deriving spatially constrained cluster by using skater() method of spdep package.

7.1 Converting into SpatialPolygonsDataFrame
First, we need to convert shan_sf into SpatialPolygonsDataFrame. This is because SKATER function only support sp objects such as SpatialPolygonDataFrame.
as_Spatial() of sf package will be used to convert shan_sf into a SpatialPolygonDataFrame called shan_sp.

shan_sp <- as_Spatial(shan_sf)



7.2 Computing Neighbour List
poly2nd() of spdep package will be used to compute the neighbours list from polygon list.

shan.nb <- poly2nb(shan_sp)

Since we now can plot the community area boundaries as well, we plot this graph on top of the map. The first plot command gives the boundaries. This is followed by the plot of the neighbor list object, with coordinates applied to the original SpatialPolygonDataFrame (Shan state township boundaries) to extract the centroids of the polygons. These are used as the nodes for the graph representation. We also set the color to blue and specify add=TRUE to plot the network on top of the boundaries.

coords <- st_coordinates(
  st_centroid(st_geometry(shan_sf)))

plot(st_geometry(shan_sf), 
     border=grey(.5))
plot(shan.nb,
     coords, 
     col="blue", 
     add=TRUE)








Note that if the network is plotted first and then the boundaries, some of the areas will be clipped. This is because the plotting area is determined by the characteristics of the first plot. In this example, because the boundary map extends further than the graph, it is plotted first.


7.3 Computing minimum spanning tree

7.3.1 Calculating edge costs
Next, nbcosts() of spdep package is used to compute the cost of each edge. It is the distance between it nodes. This function compute this distance using a data.frame with observations vector in each node.

lcosts <- nbcosts(shan.nb, shan_ict)

For each observation, this gives the pairwise dissimilarity between its values on the five variables and the values for the neighbouring observation (from the neighbour list). Basically, this is the notion of a generalised weight for a spatial weights matrix.
Next, We will incorporate these costs into a weights object in the same way as the calculation of inverse of distance weights. In other words, we convert the neighbour list to a list weights object by specifying the just computed lcosts as the weights.
In order to achieve this, nb2listw() of spdep package is used. Note that we specify the style as B to make sure the cost values are not row-standardised.

shan.w <- nb2listw(shan.nb, 
                   lcosts, 
                   style="B")

The minimum spanning tree is computed by mean of the mstree() of spdep package.

shan.mst <- mstree(shan.w)

After computing the MST, we can check its class and dimension.

7.5 Computing spatially constrained clusters using SKATER method
The spatially constrained cluster will be computed using skater() of spdep package.

clust6 <- spdep::skater(edges = shan.mst[,1:2], 
                 data = shan_ict, 
                 method = "euclidean", 
                 ncuts = 5)

skater() takes three mandatory arguments:

The first two columns of the MST matrix (i.e. not the cost)
The data matrix (to update the costs as units are being grouped)
The number of cuts.

Note: It is set to one less than the number of clusters. So, the value specified is not the number of clusters, but the number of cuts in the graph, one less than the number of clusters.
The result of the skater() is an object of class skater.

title: 06 Geographical Segmentation with Spatially Constrained Clustering Techniques
text:
8. Spatially Constrained Clustering: ClustGeo Method
The ClustGeo R package is specifically designed for spatially constrained hierarchical clustering. It implements a Ward-like algorithm hclustgeo() that allows users to incorporate spatial contiguity constraints directly into the clustering process.

8.1 Key Concepts and Methodology
The algorithm operates using two distinct dissimilarity matrices along with a mixing parameter,

D_0 (Attribute Space): Represents dissimilarities between observations based on the attribute variables (e.g., ICT penetration rates). D_0 can be non-Euclidean, and observation weights do not need to be uniform.
D_1 (Constraint Space): Represents dissimilarities in geographical space (e.g., spatial distance or connectivity matrices).
Mixing Parameter (alpha in [0, 1]): Controls the tradeoff between attribute homogeneity and spatial contiguity. At each step, the algorithm minimizes a convex combination of the homogeneity criteria derived from D_0 and D_1.To select an optimal alpha, the choicealpha() function evaluates how spatial contiguity increases relative to the loss in attribute homogeneity, allowing users to balance spatial compactness with feature precision.



8.2 Ward-like hierarchical clustering: ClustGeo
ClustGeo package provides function called hclustgeo() to perform a typical ward-like hierarchical clustering just like hclust() covered in earlier sections.
To perform non-spatially constrained hierarchical clustering, we only need to provide the function for a dissimilarity matrix.

nongeo_cluster <- hclustgeo(proxmat)
plot(nongeo_cluster, cex = 0.5)
rect.hclust(nongeo_cluster, 
            k = 6, 
            border = 2:5)








Note that the dissimilarity matrix must be an object of class dist, i.e., an object obtained with the function dist(). F

8.2.1 Mapping the clusters formed
The clusters on a categorical area shaded map can be plotted by mapping the clusters formed.

groups <- as.factor(cutree(nongeo_cluster, k=6))

shan_sf_ngeo_cluster <- cbind(shan_sf, as.matrix(groups)) %>%
  rename(`CLUSTER` = `as.matrix.groups.`)

qtm(shan_sf_ngeo_cluster, "CLUSTER")











8.3 Spatially Constrained Hierarchical Clustering
Before we can performed spatially constrained hierarchical clustering, a spatial distance matrix will be derived by using st_distance() of sf package.

dist <- st_distance(shan_sf, shan_sf)
distmat <- as.dist(dist)

Notice that as.dist() is used to convert the data frame into matrix.
Next, choicealpha() will be used to determine a suitable value for the mixing parameter alpha.

cr <- choicealpha(proxmat, distmat, range.alpha = seq(0, 1, 0.1), K=6, graph = TRUE)















With reference to the graphs above, alpha = 0.2 will be used.

clustG <- hclustgeo(proxmat, distmat, alpha = 0.2)

Next, cutree() is used to derive the cluster object.

groups <- as.factor(cutree(clustG, k=6))

We will then join back the group list with shan_sf polygon feature data frame.

shan_sf_Gcluster <- cbind(shan_sf, as.matrix(groups)) %>%
  rename(`CLUSTER` = `as.matrix.groups.`)

We can now plot the map of the newly delineated spatially constrained clusters.

qtm(shan_sf_Gcluster, "CLUSTER")

9. Visual Interpretation of Clusters

9.1 Visualising individual clustering variable
The distribution of a clustering variable (i.e RADIO_PR) can be revealed by cluster.

ggplot(data = shan_sf_ngeo_cluster,
       aes(x = CLUSTER, y = RADIO_PR)) +
  geom_boxplot()








The boxplot reveals Cluster 3 displays the highest mean Radio Ownership Per Thousand Household. This is followed by Cluster 2, 1, 4, 6 and 5.


9.2 Multivariate Visualisation
Past studies have shown that parallel coordinate plot can be used to reveal clustering variables by cluster very effectively.

ggparcoord(data = shan_sf_ngeo_cluster, 
           columns = c(17:21), 
           scale = "globalminmax",
           alphaLines = 0.2,
           boxplot = TRUE, 
           title = "Multiple Parallel Coordinates Plots of ICT Variables by Cluster") +
  facet_grid(~ CLUSTER) + 
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 30))








The parallel coordinate plot above reveals that households in Cluster 4 townships tend to own the highest number of TV and mobile-phone. On the other hand, households in Cluster 5 tends to own the lowest of all the five ICT.
Note that the scale argument of ggparcoor() provide several methods to scale the clustering variables. They are:

std: univariately, subtract mean and divide by standard deviation.
robust: univariately, subtract median and divide by median absolute deviation.
uniminmax: univariately, scale so the minimum of the variable is zero, and the maximum is one.
globalminmax: no scaling is done; the range of the graphs is defined by the global minimum and the global maximum.
center: use uniminmax to standardise vertical height, then center each variable at a value specified by the scaleSummary param.
centerObs: use uniminmax to standardise vertical height, then center each variable at the value of the observation specified by the centerObsID param

There is no one best scaling method to use. Instead, the methods should be explored and selected based on analysis needs.
The summary statistics, such as mean, median, sd, can be computed to complement the visual interpretation using group_by() and summarise() of dplyr.

shan_sf_ngeo_cluster %>% 
  st_set_geometry(NULL) %>%
  group_by(CLUSTER) %>%
  summarise(mean_RADIO_PR = mean(RADIO_PR),
            mean_TV_PR = mean(TV_PR),
            mean_LLPHONE_PR = mean(LLPHONE_PR),
            mean_MPHONE_PR = mean(MPHONE_PR),
            mean_COMPUTER_PR = mean(COMPUTER_PR))
